analysis.body:
# Grid Queue Snapshot: What It Means for AI Infrastructure

Across five major US grid operators, nearly 8,100 generation and storage projects totaling 1.33 million megawatts sit in interconnection queues as of mid-September 2026. ERCOT dominates this pipeline with 438,000 MW across 1,778 requests, followed by NYISO at 319,000 MW and MISO at 300,000 MW. These numbers represent planned capacity waiting for grid study approval and connection—not current demand, but a forward-looking measure of what utilities expect will be needed. The composition matters: across all operators, solar leads fuel type, but gas and storage together account for roughly 400,000 MW of the total, a pairing that typically tracks with data center load since both provide either firm power or load-balancing capability for high-utilization facilities.

Commercial electricity sales in June 2026 totaled 54.8 million MWh across eight major states, with Texas consuming the most at 15.8 million MWh, followed by California at 10.0 million MWh. These figures represent the commercial sector broadly—which includes data centers but also offices, retail, and light industry—so they serve as a proxy rather than a direct measurement of data center consumption. Price variation is stark: California's average commercial rate was 27.33 dollars per MWh, nearly triple Oregon's 10.59 dollars per MWh, suggesting that data center location economics remain heavily weighted toward lower-cost regions like Texas (8.66 dollars per MWh) and the Pacific Northwest.

Storage queues signal sustained regional demand expectations: ERCOT shows 160,000 MW of storage in queue, MISO 67,000 MW, and SPP 52,500 MW, while CAISO's 46,900 MW storage request reflects both the state's renewable integration challenge and existing constraints. Watch whether gas queue entries in ERCOT and SPP begin declining relative to storage as data center operators and utilities commit to firm clean power contracts, since that shift would signal a transition in how infrastructure is being planned for high-density compute clusters.
